extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, botanists, and readers of the Royal Society (17th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for making, recording, interpreting, and reporting observational natural-philosophy work (astronomical observations, plant anatomy, and optical experiments) for publication or communication to learned peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the seed and follow the series of vegetation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice that investigators should 'begin, and so proceed till the end again, with the seed' and 'confine not their inquiries to one time of the year, but to make them in several seasons'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the life-cycle from seed through root, trunk, branch, leaf, flower, fruit, and back to seed; perform observations across multiple seasons to see parts in different states; do not study only at one stage or season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators are advised 'that they neglect not the comparative anatomy, confronting several vegetables and their several parts together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare homologous parts across multiple species/vegetables to identify shared structures, variations, and functional correspondences rather than studying a single species in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect and identify constituent organical parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissect seeds (example: garden-bean) and identify constituent parts (cuticle, parenchyma, seminal root, radicle, plume) and their relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful dissection and description of component tissues and their proportions is required; name and distinguish layers (outer coats, cuticle, parenchyma, inner seminal structures) and report their arrangement and presumed roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document structure with functional interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the observable parts of roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits (skins, cortical body, lignous body, pith, insertments, pores) and explain how these parts grow and serve functions (e.g., sap ascent, nutrition, protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond morphological listing: explain growth processes (length/breadth growth), positions and courses of pores/fibres, formation of rings, and propose mechanisms (e.g., joint subserviency of lignous and cortical bodies in sap ascent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test structural hypotheses with experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experiments to demonstrate internal continuity or function (example: Mr. Hook's experiment filling pores with mercury to show continuity of woody pores/fibres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design simple, demonstrative experiments (dye, mercury, fluid tracing) to test whether proposed internal channels are continuous/permeable and report methods and results to support structural claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert or refute anatomical features with observed evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare presence or non-existence of proposed features when evidence supports it (example: 'in none of which pores he could observe any thing that may have the true nature and use of valves; the non-existence of which he is asserting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting absence of a purported structure (valves, etc.), provide the observational basis and experiments that led to that conclusion rather than mere assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe reproductive/physiological processes with process tracing
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace the movement and transformation of sap into seed material, deposition into seed coats and secundine, and the formation/coagulation/fermentation leading to seed parenchyma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report stepwise hypotheses of material flows (coarser sap to fruit, finer sap to inner coat, filtration through membranes, coagulation and fermentation) and analogize to better-known processes where helpful (e.g., egg colliquamentum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record precise times, dates, altitudes, and corrected times for astronomical events
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide exact timings (hours, minutes, seconds), dates (with new/old style notation), altitudes and corrected times for events such as occultations, eclipses, transits, and satellite disappearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tabulated times and any corrections applied; note moments of first sighting, immersion, emersion, and any uncertainty (e.g., could be a minute earlier/later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify instrument details and apertures
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the instruments used (telescope tube length, aperture, eye-glass size—examples: 20 feet tube, 14-feet telescope with 14-inch aperture and eye-glass drawing two inches) and any other apparatus (brass octant, 9-foot radius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include instrument dimensions and configurations because these materially affect what is observed and allow others to assess resolving power and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe observing conditions and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Note sky conditions (clouds, rain, twilight, moonlight), site (city), and how these conditions affected the ability to observe (examples: clouds prevented seeing beginnings, twilight/mudglass colours produced spurious rays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always report environmental/seeing conditions and any interruptions so readers can interpret observation gaps or timing uncertainties and assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observations with predictions/tables and discuss discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare measured event times/positions with computational tables (example: Rudolphine tables) and note when tables are incorrect or when observations disagree with predictions (‘‘we found that the Rudolphine tables were not correct’’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discrepancies arise, discuss possible causes (calculation error, poor tables, instrumental limits, atmospheric effects) and quantify the difference (e.g., half an hour earlier).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for optical projection/foreshortening effects when interpreting apparent shapes and velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: When tracking sunspots and similar features, account for apparent velocity changes and apparent shape changes near the solar limb caused by projection/optical rules (example: spots appearing oblong near centre, shortening of east–west diameter near limb due to obliquity of equal arches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct interpretations of apparent motion and size by applying geometrical/optical reasoning; state the hypothesis (spots adherent to surface) and derive expected apparent motions/periods (example-derived ~27.1 days) and note how apparent velocity should diminish away from centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-validate with other observers and instrument types
rubrics_metrics.description: Note and weigh other observers' reports and instrument differences (example: Cassini, Picard, Huygens, Paris observers saw Saturn round; Hevelius and others saw ansae depending on telescope length).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observations from different observers and instruments; attribute differences to instrument resolving power or observing circumstances rather than to immediate contradiction; where possible, reconcile by noting instrument capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify optical refraction behavior within observational limits
rubrics_metrics.description: State measured/reflected rules of refraction for visual rays in glass up to ~30°: 'the refraction ... to 30 degrees of inclination, is proportional to the inclination ... the angle of the refraction ... entering into glass, is about a third part of the angle ... issuing out ... is about the half'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical ratios or functional relationships observed for refraction within stated angular ranges, and indicate the sensory/measurement limits of those claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate books and publications on content, execution, and experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess works by their novelty, execution (e.g., 'very numerous and well executed engravings'), experimental content, and overall merit while noting mistakes ('though by no means free from mistakes ... a work of very considerable merit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In book notices/reviews, balance praise for ingenuity and useful features (illustrations, schemes) with candid notes of mistakes; point readers to specific strengths (e.g., useful engravings, inventive arrangements) and weaknesses.
